citation: Garrison, D. Randy, Terry Anderson, & Walter Archer. (1999). Critical Inquiry in a Text-Based Environment: Computer Conferencing in Higher Education. The Internet and Higher Education, 2(2–3), 87–105.
citationNote: Journal-issue year per manifest = 1999; the article's own page footer reads 'Copyright © 2000 Elsevier Science Inc.' — a common publisher-copyright-vs-issue-date discrepancy, not resolved further here (flag only, not blocking).
thesis: A worthwhile educational transaction requires a Community of Inquiry composed of teachers and students interacting through three interdependent elements — cognitive presence, social presence, and teaching presence — and a transcript-derived coding template of textual indicators can operationalize each element for research and practice in computer-mediated communication (CMC), particularly asynchronous computer conferencing, in higher education; this article is the keystone of a larger, ongoing research program and offers its central claim (that computer conferencing has considerable potential to create an educational community of inquiry) tentatively rather than as a demonstrated empirical result.

sections.title: Abstract and introduction to the three-element model
sections.summary: States the study's purpose as providing conceptual order and an analytic tool for CMC/computer conferencing in education. Introduces the Community of Inquiry (Fig. 1) as teachers and students interacting through cognitive presence, social presence, and teaching presence; previews the transcript-derived indicator template (Table 1). Frames the article as the keystone of a multi-article research program.

sections.title: Oral and Text-based Communication
sections.summary: Contrasts oral communication (fast, spontaneous, paralinguistically rich) with text-based communication (a 'lean' medium lacking non-verbal cues but affording time for reflection); surveys literature associating writing with more explicit, higher-order thinking while cautioning the connection is not straightforward.

sections.title: A Conceptual Framework
sections.summary: Grounds the model in Lipman's community-of-inquiry pedagogy, Ramsden's negotiation-of-meaning emphasis, and Dewey's psychological/sociological duality of education; introduces the 'collaborative constructivist perspective' and positions teaching presence as responsible for designing and integrating the cognitive and social elements.

sections.title: Cognitive Presence
sections.summary: Defines cognitive presence as the extent to which participants construct meaning through sustained communication, tied to critical thinking as higher education's ostensible goal. Reviews prior transcript-coding studies (Newman et al. 1996/1997; Gunawardena, Lowe & Anderson 1997; Bullen 1997/1998); introduces the practical inquiry model (triggering event, exploration, integration, resolution) built on Dewey's phases of inquiry.

sections.title: Social Presence
sections.summary: Defines social presence as participants' ability to project themselves socially and emotionally as 'real' people; departs from media-richness theorists (Short, Williams & Christie 1976; Daft & Lengel 1986; Sproull & Kiesler 1986), locating social presence in communication context rather than medium properties. Sets out three indicator categories (emotional expression, open communication, group cohesion) and discusses emoticons/self-disclosure as compensations for lost visual cues, citing Gunawardena & Zittle (1997).

sections.title: Teaching Presence
sections.summary: Identifies two functions (design, facilitation) and three indicator categories (instructional management, building understanding, direct instruction); argues teaching presence is the 'binding element' integrating cognitive and social presence; cites Tagg & Dickenson (1995) and Fabro & Garrison (1998) on tutor/moderator effects.

sections.title: A Template / Coding
sections.summary: Describes development of the coding template (Table 1) applying category-level indicators to each element; flags the unit-of-analysis problem as a major methodological challenge deferred to a companion paper (Rourke et al., 1999).

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Summarizes the study's contribution as a conceptual framework plus a coding template for analyzing CMC transcripts. States computer conferencing shows considerable potential for creating an educational community of inquiry, while much work remains on optimal design and delivery.

constructs.treatment: extent to which participants construct meaning through sustained communication; most basic element to educational success; operationalized via the four-phase practical inquiry model (triggering event, exploration, integration, resolution)

constructs.label: teaching presence (THEORY-MODEL component, related but distinct)
constructs.treatment: the 'binding element'; two functions (design, facilitation), three indicator categories (instructional management, building understanding, direct instruction)

constructs.treatment: the composite structure — teachers and students interacting via the three presences — within which a worthwhile educational experience is embedded (Fig. 1)

constructs.treatment: analogical only — approached via 'group cohesion' and the hypothesis that high social presence with commitment/participation is necessary for higher-order thinking; not named or measured as a distinct construct

conditionsNote: Empty by design. This is a conceptual/theoretical framework paper proposing a model and a transcript-derived coding template; it reports no sample, N, instrument validation, or statistical findings of its own (the coding template is explicitly described as at a 'preliminary application' stage, to be verified in future studies). No media-condition axis content: all communication described is asynchronous, text-based computer conferencing; there is no IVR, desktop-3D, or 2D-video contrast, and no conventional-instruction control arm. Strand F is not required to populate the §3 media-condition column per plan scope, and nothing in this source genuinely fits any of its eight canonical labels.

readings.claim: Computer conferencing shows considerable potential to create an educational community of inquiry, though much work remains to determine how a worthwhile educational experience can be optimally designed and delivered in a text-based environment.

Social presence is participants' capacity to present their full, genuine personalities — socially and emotionally, as 'real' people rather than anonymous senders of text — through whatever communication medium is in use.

Cognitive presence — the extent to which participants construct meaning through sustained communication — is most basic to educational success but is not by itself sufficient to sustain a critical community of learners.

High levels of social presence, with accompanying high degrees of commitment and participation, are hypothesized to be necessary for the development of higher-order thinking skills and collaborative work.

Unlike earlier communications theorists (Daft & Lengel 1986; Short, Williams & Christie 1976; Sproull & Kiesler 1986), the effect of media per se is not the most salient factor in determining social presence; communication context (familiarity, skills, motivation, organizational commitment, activities, duration of use) directly influences it.

Teaching presence is the binding element integrating cognitive and social presence toward educational outcomes; failures in computer-conferencing-based education are usually attributed to a deficit of teaching presence rather than the medium.
Conference participants enhanced their socio-emotional experience by using emoticons to express missing nonverbal cues in written form (quoting Gunawardena & Zittle, 1997, p.8).

Computer-conferencing students demonstrated higher-quality critical-thinking indicators (linking outside material, applying solutions) than face-to-face seminar students but were less interactive overall (reporting Newman et al. 1996, 1997).
The coding template's chief unresolved methodological problem is the unit-of-analysis question, deferred to a companion paper (Rourke et al., 1999).

concepts.definition: The composite structure of teachers and students interacting through cognitive presence, social presence, and teaching presence within which a worthwhile educational experience is embedded (Fig. 1).
The extent to which participants in a community of inquiry are able to construct meaning through sustained communication; the most basic of the three elements.
Participants' capacity to present themselves as genuine, full 'real' people — socially and emotionally — through whatever communication medium is in use.
Two general functions — design of the educational experience and facilitation — that bind cognitive and social presence toward educational outcomes.
A four-phase model of cognitive presence (triggering event, exploration, integration, resolution) built on Dewey's pre-reflection/reflection/post-reflection phases of inquiry.
Garrison & Archer's (in press) framing of an educational experience as a collaborative communication process for constructing meaningful, worthwhile knowledge.
The four coding categories operationalizing cognitive presence in the transcript template.

concepts.term: emotional expression / open communication / group cohesion
concepts.definition: The three coding categories operationalizing social presence in the transcript template.

concepts.term: instructional management / building understanding / direct instruction
concepts.definition: The three coding categories operationalizing teaching presence in the transcript template.

interlocutors.name: Dewey, John
interlocutors.role: source of practical inquiry's pre-reflection/reflection/post-reflection phases; general claim that education has inseparable psychological and sociological sides

interlocutors.name: Lipman, Matthew
interlocutors.role: source of the community-of-inquiry pedagogy concept, glossed via questioning/reasoning/connecting/deliberating/challenging

interlocutors.name: Ramsden, Paul
interlocutors.role: cited for the importance of negotiating meaning and challenging accepted beliefs in deep, meaningful learning

interlocutors.name: Short, John, Ederyn Williams & Bruce Christie (1976)
interlocutors.role: media-richness/social-presence theorists whose medium-determines-presence position this article explicitly departs from

interlocutors.name: Daft, Richard L. & Robert H. Lengel (1986)
interlocutors.role: media-richness theorists, cited alongside Short/Williams/Christie as the departed-from position

interlocutors.name: Sproull, Lee & Sara Kiesler (1986)
interlocutors.role: media-richness theorists ('reducing social context cues'), cited alongside the above

interlocutors.name: Walther, Joseph
interlocutors.role: cited for CMC users' compensating linguistic/textual behaviors when visual cues are reduced or eliminated

interlocutors.name: Schrage, Michael
interlocutors.role: cited on collaboration as an act of shared creation/discovery and on technology shaping how people relate

interlocutors.name: Gunawardena, Charlotte N. & Frank J. Zittle (1997)
interlocutors.role: cited directly for the finding that conference participants used emoticons to compensate for missing nonverbal cues — this cluster's ped-sec-25, the one intra-cluster citation this 1999 article could actually make

interlocutors.name: Newman, D. R., Johnson, C., Cochrane, C. & Webb, B. (1996, 1997)
interlocutors.role: prior empirical transcript-comparison study of face-to-face vs. computer-conference critical thinking, reported as background evidence

tensions.axis: presence as technology-determined (medium properties) vs. presence as psychologically/individually determined (communication context)
tensions.note: The article's central theoretical move: an explicit, named departure from media-richness theorists (Short, Williams & Christie 1976; Daft & Lengel 1986; Sproull & Kiesler 1986), relocating social presence in familiarity, skills, motivation, organizational commitment, and duration of use rather than in the medium itself. Lands directly on the cluster plan's debate axis 3.

tensions.axis: cognitive presence as sufficient vs. cognitive presence requiring social-emotional support
tensions.note: Cognitive presence is 'most basic' but explicitly 'not sufficient to sustain a critical community of learners' on its own; must be nurtured within a broader socio-emotional environment (social presence).

tensions.axis: CMC critical-thinking quality vs. CMC interactivity/volume
tensions.note: Reporting Newman et al. (1996, 1997): computer-conferencing students showed higher-quality critical-thinking indicators but were less interactive and less creative in volume than face-to-face seminar students — an unresolved trade-off the article itself flags rather than adjudicates.

bridgeNote: vle-01's F7 finding ('Presence & the WE': F1-PRESENCE indicator rate 4.3 vs 1.2 per-100 postings, APP vs VID strata; E-SHA optative language such as 'seemed isolating'; 'watch with others' cited as a main pro) and vle-03's exemplar quotes on presence, carry-over, and social watching plausibly instantiate this article's social-presence construct (participants projecting themselves as 'real people') within the VLE's own text data, even though the VLE's medium (3D app vs. solo video) differs from this article's medium (asynchronous text conferencing) — the construct transfers across media, the operationalization does not (P/anticipatory-application). The article's own departure from media-richness theory (locating social presence in communication context rather than medium properties) offers Part III a theoretical resource for interpreting the VLE's APP/VID presence-indicator gap without attributing it to the video medium's technological 'leanness' alone.
hubNote: Foundational Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework paper (cognitive presence / social presence / teaching presence). Very likely the single most-cited external interlocutor within Strand F. Flag: Terry & Doolittle 'Re-examining Social Presence' (ped-sec-31, 2019) is the single most probable direct citer given its explicit re-examination framing of this article's construct; Richardson & Swan (ped-sec-28, 2003) and Richardson et al.'s meta-analysis (ped-sec-32, 2017) are the next most probable, sitting downstream of the CoI research program this article inaugurates; Tu (ped-sec-27, 2002), Biocca, Burgoon & Harms (ped-sec-29, 2003), and Kreijns, Kirschner & Jochems (ped-sec-30, 2003) are plausible but less certain citers. This article's own citations run the other direction (backward to Gunawardena & Zittle 1997, ped-sec-25), since it predates every other Strand-F unit except that one.
